statement: In adults who regularly consumed a lot of caffeine and went without it while fasting for minor surgery, going without caffeine increases headache: half of those given placebo tablets (10 of 20) reported a headache by the evening of the day of surgery and 7 of 20 the next morning, against none and 1 of 20 of those given caffeine tablets instead, in a double-blind randomized trial (Hampl et al., 1995); the difference on the evening was 50 percentage points (editors' calculation, 95% CI 24 to 70). Nausea, tiredness, vomiting and unsteadiness did not differ detectably. The trial was small and in a hospital, where anaesthesia and fasting may add to headache, and it excluded smokers and people with frequent headaches. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: People who usually had a lot of caffeine and went without it for surgery often had a headache by the evening; those given their caffeine as tablets mostly did not.
population: 40 adults aged about 20 to 65 (27 women) who regularly consumed a lot of caffeine (study threshold on the study card), non-smokers without frequent headaches, having minor surgery under general anaesthesia in Basel
exposure: Going without caffeine from the preoperative visit to the next morning, with placebo tablets
comparator: The same caffeine abstinence with caffeine tablets instead of placebo (double-blind; study amounts on the study card)
outcome: Headache (yes or no) and other possible withdrawal symptoms on a checklist before anaesthesia, on the evening of surgery and the next morning
magnitude: Evening of surgery: headache in 10 of 20 with placebo against 0 of 20 with caffeine (P < 0.001); editors' calculation: risk difference 50 percentage points (95% CI 24 to 70), Fisher's exact p = 0.0004. Next morning: 7 of 20 against 1 of 20 (P < 0.05); risk difference 30 percentage points (5 to 52), p = 0.044. Before anaesthesia: 1 of 20 against 0 of 20.

risk_of_bias.note: Sequence generation and attrition not reported, no protocol, and several reporting errors (card overall: some concerns).

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for regular caffeine consumers going without caffeine around surgery; everyday caffeine withdrawal outside hospital was not studied.

imprecision.note: 40 patients and few events; the next-morning difference is fragile (exact p = 0.044).

grade.reasoning: A randomized double-blind trial starts high; downgraded for risk of bias and imprecision, giving low. Because caffeine replacement was randomized and blinded, the excess headache in the placebo group can be attributed to going without caffeine rather than to surgery or anaesthesia, which both groups had. The same trial supports the claim on caffeine tablets around surgery (section 12); the two claims share one evidence base and must not be counted as two studies.
